title: Tamagoyaki
subtitle: Japanese sweet rolled omelette
excerpt: Tamagoyaki is a layered Japanese omelette made by rolling thin sheets of seasoned egg in a pan. The result is a firm, slightly sweet log that is sliced into rounds. It is a core part of Japanese bento boxes and sushi sets.
sourceNotes: Tamagoyaki is a Japanese sweet rolled omelette. The technique of rolling successive thin layers of egg in a rectangular pan (tamagoyaki-ki) has been refined over centuries. It is a key component of Japanese bento boxes and sushi sets, and a popular home breakfast dish.

content.text: The technique for tamagoyaki is the same each time: pour, spread, roll while still slightly wet. The key is to roll before the egg sets fully -- if you wait too long it cracks instead of rolling. A small non-stick pan makes this much easier than a regular frying pan.
Beat the eggs with the soy sauce, honey, and salt until well combined.
Heat a small frying pan (or tamagoyaki pan) over medium heat. Add a thin film of oil.
Pour in a third of the egg mixture. Tilt the pan to spread it evenly. When the egg is just set but still slightly wet on top, use a spatula to roll it from one end to the other.
Push the roll to one end of the pan. Add another third of egg mixture, lifting the roll so the liquid egg runs underneath. When set, roll the new layer around the first roll.
Repeat with the remaining egg. You will have a layered log shape. Remove from the pan and roll tightly in a sheet of baking paper. Leave to cool for 2 minutes, then slice into rounds.

items.cause: Egg too well-done before rolling, or heat too high
items.fix: Roll the egg while it is still slightly wet on top. Keep the heat at medium -- the egg should set slowly enough to stay flexible.

content.text: Tamagoyaki is a staple of Japanese bento boxes. The layers of sweetened rolled egg look impressive but the technique is straightforward once you practise a few times. In Japan, the ratio of sweet to savoury varies by region -- Kansai-style is sweeter than Kanto-style.
